title: The Story of the Iliad
author: Alfred J. Church
openingText: Leda, Queen of Sparta, bare a daughter, Helen by name, that grew to be the fairest of all women upon earth. She married Menelaus, son of Atreus, and for a while dwelt in peace with her husband, bearing him a daughter, Hermione by name. But there came to the court of Menelaus, who was by this time King of Sparta, a certain Paris, second in birth among the sons of Priam, King of Troy.
about:
This is a prose retelling of Homer’s Iliad for young readers by Alfred John Church (1829–1912), in the Macmillan edition of 1920 that Project Gutenberg digitised. It follows the story of the last year of the siege of Troy: the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, the duels and battles, the death of Patroclus, the killing of Hector, and the ransom of his body by his father Priam.

Church keeps Homer’s order of events and many of his repeated phrases, but he writes in plain narrative English. Greek names follow the older English forms used in the text (Ulysses, Hector, Achilles). Short pronunciation notes appear in the text as footnotes. This is a retelling, not a translation of the Greek.

whyItMatters.title: Anger drives the whole poem
whyItMatters.body: The Iliad begins with Achilles’ anger and follows its consequences through two armies. The poem asks what a hero owes his side when he feels insulted. Church’s retelling keeps that structure intact. The question still reads as modern in any story about pride and loyalty.

whyItMatters.title: Both sides are given grief
whyItMatters.body: The Trojans are not villains in this retelling. Hector says goodbye to his wife and son, and Priam kneels to ask Achilles for his son’s body. The poem lets enemies mourn alike. Readers can see why this scene has been retold for centuries.

whyItMatters.title: The gods take sides
whyItMatters.body: Athene, Apollo, Hera and Zeus steer events, protect favorites and quarrel among themselves. Mortals act, but the outcome often depends on a god’s decision. Watching how the gods interfere shows how the ancient Greeks explained luck and fate.

angleCards.title: Follow Achilles’ anger
angleCards.text: Track what angers Achilles, what he refuses, and what finally changes his mind.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Iliad to follow how Achilles’ anger drives the events of the war.

angleCards.title: Read the two sides
angleCards.text: Notice how the Trojans and the Greeks are shown, and where each side earns sympathy.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Iliad to compare how Greeks and Trojans are portrayed.

angleCards.title: Watch the gods
angleCards.text: Note each time a god helps or hinders a mortal and what that suggests about fate.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Iliad to see how the gods shape the fighting and the heroes’ choices.

angleCards.title: Meet the heroes by their deeds
angleCards.text: Compare Diomed, Ajax, Hector, Ulysses and Achilles by how they fight and speak.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Story of the Iliad to compare the heroes by what they do.
